title: Aquinas's Five Ways
note: In Summa Theologiae I, q. 2, a. 3, Aquinas gives five short proofs from effects to their first cause: from motion, efficient causation, contingency, degrees of perfection, and the directedness of nature. The regresses he rules out are essentially ordered ones, where each cause acts only while being acted on, so the Ways do not assume the universe had a beginning.

read.title: The First Way
text: Aquinas calls the argument from motion 'the first and more manifest way.' By motion he means any change in which something potential becomes actual, as wood that is potentially hot becomes actually hot when fire heats it. The argument runs:

(1) Some things are in motion, that is, are being changed. (2) Whatever is changed is changed by something else, since nothing can be both potential and actual in the same respect at once. (3) If that mover is itself being changed, it too is changed by another. (4) This series cannot go on to infinity, for then there would be no first mover, and so no other mover either. (5) Therefore there is a first mover, moved by no other, 'and this everyone understands to be God.'
A common objection is that an infinite regress is perfectly possible. Aquinas himself held that reason cannot prove the world had a beginning; an endless line of ancestors is not absurd.

The reply turns on the kind of series in view. In an essentially ordered series, like a staff moved by a hand, each member moves only while it is being moved here and now. Such members have no power of their own to pass along. Lengthening the chain, even infinitely, explains nothing unless something actual, which needs no actualizing, sustains the whole. The First Way concerns this kind of series, not a chain stretching back in time.

o: Any change from potential to actual

q.q: Why can an essentially ordered series not explain itself?
o: Its members have no causal power of their own to pass along
It must have begun at a date in the past
It always contains only finitely many members

q.q: What did Aquinas think reason cannot prove?
o: That the world had a beginning
